groups.high: Plagiarism presents another person's words, ideas, data, or other contribution as one's own without appropriate acknowledgment. It can occur even when copyright permission exists, because academic attribution and copyright are different obligations. Conversely, citation alone does not authorize every copyrighted use. UNESCO's 2017 Recommendation on Science and Scientific Researchers supports integrity and responsible research governance; it does not impose one automatic worldwide penalty of credit cancellation, suspension, or degree loss for every case. Institutions apply their own lawful misconduct rules, which may distinguish errors, negligent practice, deliberate copying, severity, and repetition. Fair procedures should identify the allegation and evidence, permit a response, and provide applicable review or appeal. Similarity software is a screening tool, not conclusive proof of plagiarism or its absence. Quote copied language, cite the actual source, paraphrase genuinely, and keep clear notes separating borrowed material from original work. Follow the institution's rules for collaboration, reuse, and AI assistance. If accused, preserve drafts and sources, request the relevant policy and evidence, and respond within deadlines. Proportionate correction and education can matter alongside disciplinary action.
groups.mid: Plagiarism means passing off someone else's words, ideas, data, or work as your own without proper credit. Copyright permission does not remove the need for academic credit. Credit alone does not make every use lawful either. UNESCO's 2017 Recommendation on Science and Scientific Researchers supports honest research. It does not set one automatic world penalty. Loss of credits, suspension, or degree loss depends on lawful local rules and the case. Schools may consider errors, careless work, deliberate copying, seriousness, and repeat acts. A fair process should tell you the claim and show evidence. You should get a chance to reply and use any review or appeal. A similarity score is a clue, not proof of guilt or innocence. Quote copied words and cite the real source. Use your own words to paraphrase, but still give credit. Keep clear notes on what is borrowed. Follow rules on group work, reuse, and AI tools. If accused, keep drafts and sources. Ask for the policy and evidence. Reply on time. Fair correction and learning can matter as well as punishment.
groups.low: Plagiarism means passing off someone else's work as your own. It can involve words, ideas, data, or other work without proper credit. Permission to copy does not remove the need for academic credit. Credit alone does not make every use lawful under copyright. UNESCO's 2017 Recommendation on Science and Scientific Researchers supports honest research. It does not set one automatic world penalty. Loss of credits, suspension, or degree loss depends on lawful local rules and the case. Schools may check intent, care, severity, and repeat acts. A fair process should tell you the claim and show the evidence. You should have a chance to reply and use any review or appeal. A similarity score is not proof that you did or did not plagiarize. Put copied words in quotes and name the real source. When you use your own wording for an idea, still give credit. Keep clear notes on what is borrowed. Follow rules on group work, reuse, and AI help. If accused, keep drafts and sources. Ask for the policy and evidence. Reply on time. Correction and learning may matter as well as discipline.
groups.source_review: Checked UNESCO recommendation scope; no institution-specific sanctions asserted. Recordkeeping and procedure recommendations identified as practical safeguards.
groups.notes: Corrected fabricated mandatory sanctions and confusion between academic credit and copyright permission.

groups.high: Education fee transparency means giving prospective and enrolled students understandable information about mandatory charges, optional services, payment dates, changes, and refund conditions. It supports informed choices and can expose discriminatory or unauthorized charges, but does not itself guarantee affordability. UNESCO's 1960 Convention against Discrimination in Education addresses unequal treatment; Article 3(c) concerns differences by public authorities between nationals in school fees and assistance except on grounds of merit or need. It does not establish a universal approved-price schedule or prohibit every fee increase by every private institution. Domestic education law, accreditation conditions, consumer law, funding rules, and the enrollment agreement determine specific requirements. Request an itemized written fee schedule covering tuition, examinations, registration, accommodation, and any compulsory extras. Check which costs can change, how notice works, and the basis for refunds or withdrawal charges. Keep the published schedule, offer, agreement, receipts, and later demands. If a charge differs, ask for its authority and calculation and use the institution's complaint process or relevant regulator. Targeted assistance based on need or merit is not automatically unlawful unequal treatment. Compare total costs rather than headline tuition alone.
groups.mid: Clear fees help students know what they must pay. Explain required charges, optional services, due dates, changes, and refunds. This helps choices and can reveal unfair or unauthorized charges. It does not make school affordable by itself. UNESCO's 1960 Convention against Discrimination in Education deals with unequal treatment. Article 3(c) covers differences by public authorities between nationals in school fees and assistance. Merit or need can justify differences. The treaty does not set one approved price list for every school. It does not ban all private-school fee rises. Local education and consumer law, accreditation, funding rules, and the enrollment agreement decide the details. Ask for an itemized written schedule. Include tuition, exams, registration, housing, and required extras. Check what can change, notice, refunds, and withdrawal costs. Keep the schedule, offer, agreement, receipts, and later bills. If a charge differs, ask what rule allows it and how it was worked out. Use the school complaint route or regulator if needed. Aid based on need or merit is not automatically unfair. Compare the full cost, not just tuition.
groups.low: Clear fee information helps you know what to pay. It should cover required charges, optional services, due dates, changes, and refunds. It helps you choose and spot unfair or unauthorized charges. It does not make school affordable by itself. UNESCO's 1960 Convention against Discrimination in Education deals with unequal treatment. Article 3(c) covers differences by public authorities between nationals in school fees and assistance. Merit or need can justify differences. The Convention does not set one approved price list for every institution. It does not ban all private-school fee rises. Local education and consumer law, accreditation, funding rules, and your enrollment agreement decide the details. Ask for a written list of costs. Include tuition, exams, registration, housing, and required extras. Check what can change, notice, refunds, and withdrawal charges. Keep the schedule, offer, agreement, receipts, and later bills. If a charge differs, ask what rule allows it and how it was worked out. Use the school's complaint route if needed. The regulator may help too. Aid based on need or merit is not automatically unfair. Compare the whole cost, not just tuition.
groups.source_review: Read Convention Article3(c) and scope. Domestic approved rates not supplied by original and not invented.
groups.notes: Corrected universal price-control claim and distinguished nondiscrimination from identical fees for all circumstances.

groups.high: Where the GDPR applies, a university must process student data lawfully, fairly, transparently, and for specified purposes. Admissions data cannot be freely sold or reused merely because the institution holds it. A suitable Article 6 basis is required; sensitive data may also require an Article 9 condition. Purpose compatibility and other safeguards matter if a new use is proposed. Consent is not the only possible basis, but where relied upon it must meet the law's requirements and not be coerced through unnecessary conditions. Commercial suppliers can lawfully provide contracted services under appropriate controller–processor arrangements; that is not identical to selling student profiles for unrelated marketing. Universities should minimize data, limit retention and access, use appropriate security, and explain purposes and recipients. Transfers outside the EEA require the relevant legal transfer mechanism where applicable, not always the same contractual clauses. Students may have access, correction, objection, erasure, or restriction rights subject to conditions and exceptions. High-risk processing can require a data-protection impact assessment. Fines, damages, and complaint outcomes depend on the actual infringement; they are not automatic. Contact the university's data-protection officer or competent regulator about suspected misuse.
groups.mid: Where GDPR applies, a university must use student data lawfully, fairly, clearly, and for stated purposes. It cannot freely sell admission details or use them as it likes. Article 6 requires a lawful basis. Sensitive data may also need an Article 9 condition. New uses must meet purpose rules and other safeguards. Consent is not the only basis. If relied on, it must be valid and not forced by needless conditions. A paid supplier may run a service under a proper data contract. This differs from selling profiles for unrelated adverts. Collect no needless data. Limit how long it is kept and who sees it. Protect records and explain purposes and recipients. Sending data outside the EEA requires the right transfer mechanism where applicable. It is not always one type of contract. Students may have rights to access, correction, objection, erasure, or restriction. Conditions and exceptions apply. High-risk use may need an impact assessment. Fines and damages depend on what happened. Ask the university's privacy officer or regulator about misuse.
groups.low: Where GDPR applies, a university must use student data fairly and lawfully. It must say what the data is for. It cannot sell entry details or use them as it likes. Article 6 needs a lawful basis. For sensitive data, Article 9 may add a condition too. New uses must meet rules on purpose and safeguards. Consent is not the only basis. If used, it must be valid, not forced by needless conditions. A paid firm may run a service under a proper data contract. This is not selling profiles for unrelated adverts. Keep no needless data. Limit who sees it and how long it is kept. Protect it. Say who gets it. Data sent outside the EEA needs the right legal route where applicable. It is not always the same contract. Students may ask for access and to fix errors. They may object, ask to erase data, or limit use under conditions and exceptions. High-risk use may need an impact assessment. Fines are not fixed for every case. Nor are damages. Ask the university's privacy officer about misuse. A regulator may help too.
groups.source_review: Checked GDPR principles, bases, processors, rights, transfers and assessment rules. Did not assert an absolute commercial-supplier ban.
groups.notes: Corrected absolute commercial sharing prohibition, every-purpose-violation claim, and universal transfer-clause requirement.

groups.high: Bangladesh's Constitution distinguishes related equality protections. Article 27 provides equality before law and equal protection of law. Article 28(1) prohibits State discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. Article 28(3) addresses restrictions on citizens' admission to educational institutions on those grounds only. Article 28(4) permits specified special provisions for women, children, or advancement of backward sections; equality does not prohibit every targeted support measure. Public-employment equality is principally addressed by Article 29, not by the admission clause. These provisions do not themselves prescribe automatic withdrawal of a school's or professional's license for every disputed admission. Institutional rules, lawful admission criteria, applicable statutes, and available remedies must be examined. Preserve the application, eligibility requirements, rejection, communications, and evidence of discriminatory treatment. Ask for written reasons and seek timely advice about an internal appeal, regulator complaint, legal aid, or constitutional remedy where appropriate. A rejection alone does not prove discrimination, but stated policies or unequal treatment can be relevant evidence. Do not confuse constitutional protection with an invented automatic penalty.
groups.mid: Bangladesh's Constitution has linked rules on equal treatment. Article 27 gives equality before law and equal protection of law. Article 28(1) says the State must not discriminate on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. Article 28(3) covers citizens' admission to schools and other places of learning on those grounds only. Article 28(4) allows special measures for women, children, or advancement of backward sections. Equal treatment does not ban all such help. Article 29 mainly covers public jobs, not admission. These clauses do not mean a school or professional license is lost at once after every dispute. Local laws, lawful entry rules, and remedies must be checked. Keep the application, entry rules, refusal, and messages. Keep evidence of unequal treatment too. Ask for written reasons. Get prompt advice on an appeal, regulator complaint, legal aid, or a court remedy where suitable. Rejection alone is not proof of discrimination. A stated unfair rule or different treatment may be evidence. Do not confuse a real right with a fixed penalty not stated in law.
groups.low: Bangladesh's Constitution has rules for fair treatment. Article 27 gives equality before law and equal protection of law. Article 28(1) bars State discrimination. The listed grounds are religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth only. Article 28(3) uses those grounds only for citizens' admission to schools or other places of learning. Article 28(4) allows some special help. It covers women, children, or advancement of backward sections. Equal treatment does not ban all such help. Article 29 mainly covers public jobs. These rules do not mean a school or professional loses a license at once after each dispute. Check local law and lawful entry rules. Check what help the law gives. Keep the entry form and rules. Keep the refusal and messages. Keep proof of unequal treatment. Ask for reasons in writing. Get advice soon. You may appeal or complain to a regulator. Legal aid or a court may help. A refusal alone is not proof of bias. An unfair rule or different treatment may be evidence. A real right does not mean a fixed penalty.
groups.source_review: Read Constitution Articles27–29 directly; remedies and penalties left to applicable procedures.
groups.notes: Corrected article content and fabricated automatic license revocation.

groups.high: The Convention on the Rights of the Child protects children against physical and mental violence in Article 19. Article 28(2) requires school discipline consistent with the child's human dignity. The CRC Committee's General Comment 8 addresses corporal punishment and other cruel or degrading punishment, and General Comment 13 addresses freedom from violence. A claim that General Comment 13 is a 2011 education-specific text should be corrected. Corporal punishment uses physical force intended to cause pain or discomfort, however light; humiliation and degrading nonphysical discipline also raise rights concerns. Calling violence discipline does not remove the harm or excuse it. States must implement protection through laws, safeguards, reporting, training, and effective responses, while exact domestic offences and procedures vary. Positive, nonviolent discipline can teach boundaries without hitting, threats, or public shame. If a child is at risk, prioritize immediate safety and appropriate medical care, document facts without exposing the child unnecessarily, and contact the school's safeguarding route or relevant child-protection authority. Avoid confronting an alleged abuser alone if this increases danger. A report should trigger fair, child-sensitive handling, not retaliation. Violence is not required for a safe learning environment.
groups.mid: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child has protection from physical and mental violence in Article 19. Article 28(2) says school discipline must respect a child's dignity. The CRC Committee's General Comment 8 covers corporal punishment and cruel or degrading punishment. General Comment 13 is about freedom from violence. It is not a special 2011 school text. Corporal punishment uses force meant to cause pain or discomfort, however light. Public shame and degrading acts may also violate rights. Calling it discipline does not excuse violence. States need laws and safeguards. They need reporting, training, and action. Exact local offences and steps differ. Positive, nonviolent methods can teach limits without hitting, threats, or shame. If a child is unsafe, protect them first. Get medical care if needed. Note facts without exposing the child needlessly. Tell school safeguarding staff or the relevant child-protection authority. Do not face an alleged abuser alone if that raises danger. Reports need fair, child-sensitive handling, not retaliation. A safe school does not need violence.
groups.low: Children have a right to be safe from violence. Article 19 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child covers physical and mental violence. Article 28(2) says school discipline must respect a child's dignity. The CRC Committee's General Comment 8 deals with corporal punishment and cruel or degrading punishment. General Comment 13 deals with freedom from violence. It is not a special 2011 school text. This punishment means force meant to cause pain or discomfort. It counts even if light. Shame and other acts that degrade a child may harm rights too. Calling it discipline is no excuse. States need laws, safeguards, reports, training, and action. Local offences differ. So do the steps. Teach limits without hitting, threats, or shame. If a child is at risk, keep them safe first. Get medical care if needed. Keep notes without exposing them needlessly. Tell school staff who handle safety. Or tell the child-protection authority. Do not face an alleged abuser alone if that adds risk. Reports need fair handling that puts the child first. No one should face punishment for making a report. Schools do not need violence.
groups.source_review: Checked CRC Articles19,28(2) and Committee general-comment identities. Domestic reporting authorities left jurisdiction-specific.
groups.notes: Corrected General Comment misidentification and avoided unsupported exact psychological-outcome claims.

groups.high: The Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities requires inclusive education and equal access without disability discrimination. Article 24(5) addresses general tertiary education, vocational training, adult education, and lifelong learning, including reasonable accommodation. Article 2 defines accommodation as necessary and appropriate adjustments for a particular case that do not impose a disproportionate or undue burden. It is distinct from a numerical admissions quota and from anticipatory accessibility duties. Depending on the student's needs, measures can include accessible materials, sign-language support, assistive technology, adjustments to examination arrangements, or accessible facilities. Essential academic competencies remain relevant; accommodation should enable demonstration of them rather than equate disability with inability. The CRPD does not set one worldwide percentage of reserved university seats. India's 2016 Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act section 32 provides a separate example: at least 5% of seats in covered government or government-aided higher-education institutions for persons with benchmark disabilities, not the original claimed 2%. Quotas alone do not ensure meaningful participation. Institutions need accessible systems, individual consultation, prompt reasoned decisions, trained staff, and effective challenge routes. A generic claim of cost or inconvenience should not replace proper assessment of a requested adjustment.
groups.mid: CRPD is the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. It calls for the right to learn with others, without unfair disability-based exclusion. Article 24(5) covers college, university, job training, adult learning, and lifelong learning. It includes reasonable accommodation, or changes to help a student take part. Article 2 means changes needed for a particular person to take part, unless the burden is disproportionate or undue. These adjustments differ from an admission quota or plans for access for all. A student may need books all can use, sign-language support, assistive technology, exam changes, or suitable facilities. Support helps show key skills for the course. Disability does not mean inability. CRPD sets no fixed world percentage of university seats. India's 2016 disability-rights law gives a separate example. Section 32 sets at least 5% of seats in covered public colleges and universities or those funded by the State for persons with benchmark disabilities. It is not 2%. A seat quota alone is not inclusion. Colleges need systems all can use. They must talk with each student. Staff need training, and decisions must be timely and have reasons. Students need a way to challenge refusal, and a vague claim that cost or trouble is too great is not enough. Each student's needs must be properly checked.
groups.low: CRPD is the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. It supports the right to learn with others on equal terms. Disability should not lead to unfair exclusion. Article 24(5) covers college, university, job training, adult learning, and lifelong learning. It includes reasonable accommodation, or changes to help a student take part. Article 2 means changes needed for a person to take part. They must not impose a disproportionate or undue burden. This differs from a quota for entry or plans for access for all. Help may include books all can use, sign-language support, assistive technology, exam changes, or suitable facilities. It helps show key skills for the course. Disability does not mean inability. CRPD sets no fixed world university quota. India's 2016 disability-rights law is a separate example. Section 32 gives at least 5% of seats in covered public colleges and universities or those funded by the State to persons with benchmark disabilities. It is not 2%. A quota alone is not inclusion. Colleges need systems all can use. They must talk with each student. Staff need training, and staff must give reasons for decisions. Do not delay them. There must be a way to challenge refusal. A vague claim that cost or trouble is too great is not enough. Each student's needs must be properly checked.
groups.source_review: Checked CRPD Articles2,5,24 and General Comment4. Indian5%example checked against 2016 Act provision, not presumed global quota.
groups.notes: Corrected quota/accommodation conflation, CRPD burden wording, and Indian quota percentage.

groups.high: ICESCR Article 13 recognizes the right to education, but it does not explicitly guarantee unconditional transfer between any two institutions or automatic international admission and credit recognition. Transfer decisions can depend on lawful admission criteria, capacity, curriculum compatibility, accreditation, academic standing, and applicable rules. Procedures should be clear, nondiscriminatory, and consistent with the right to education. Records such as transcripts, transfer certificates, and course descriptions support continuity, but deadlines and any lawful fee or withholding rules require the relevant domestic framework and institutional policy. Do not claim that every delay is automatically a treaty violation or that all credits must be accepted. Ask the receiving institution what documents, eligibility, available places, and credit decisions are required before leaving the current course. Request records in writing, retain proof, and identify completion dates and appeal routes. If an institution obstructs transfer arbitrarily, request the legal or policy basis and use the appropriate grievance, regulator, or legal-aid channel. Student-data access rights may provide another route to some information where applicable, without guaranteeing that every requested certificate must be issued in a particular format.
groups.mid: ICESCR Article 13 protects the right to learn. It does not promise a transfer to any school or university, a place abroad, or acceptance of every credit. Lawful entry rules may apply. Space, course fit, accreditation, academic standing, and local rules can matter. The steps should be clear and free from discrimination. Transcripts, transfer certificates, and course details help study continue. Local rules set dates, fees, and any lawful limits on releasing papers. A delay is not always a treaty breach. Before leaving, ask the new school what it needs. Check documents, eligibility, places, and which credits count. Ask for records in writing. Keep proof and ask when they will be ready. Check appeal routes. If transfer is blocked without good reason, ask for the law or policy behind it. Use the right complaint route, regulator, or legal aid. Data-access rights may help get some facts where they apply. They do not promise every certificate in the exact form requested.
groups.low: ICESCR Article 13 protects education. It does not mean any school must take you. It does not promise a place abroad or that every credit counts. Lawful entry rules, space, course fit, accreditation, and your academic record may matter. The steps should be clear and fair. Transcripts, transfer certificates, and course details help study go on. Local rules set dates and charges. They set any lawful limits on release too. Not every delay is a treaty breach. Ask the new school what it needs before you leave. Check entry rules, places, papers, and credits. Ask for records in writing. Keep proof. Ask when they will be ready. Ask how to appeal. If transfer is blocked without good reason, ask for the law or policy. A complaint route, regulator, or legal aid may help. Data-access rights may give some facts where they apply. They do not promise every certificate in any form you want.
groups.source_review: Read ICESCR13 and example Bangladesh education-board power over transfer conditions. No invented universal transfer/certificate rule.
groups.notes: Corrected treaty attribution of unconditional transfer, automatic credit recognition, and immediate document entitlement.

groups.high: Fair assessment should measure relevant learning rather than arbitrary barriers, apply published rules consistently, and provide appropriate disability accommodations. ICESCR Article 13 recognizes education rights, but does not itself prescribe every grading rubric, feedback entitlement, or appeal procedure worldwide. Domestic education law, institutional assessment rules, and applicable equality protections determine concrete rights. Useful transparency includes the assessment format, component weights, criteria, permitted resources, deadlines, misconduct rules, and the basis for a result. Access to marked work or examiner material can have lawful limits, including other people's rights and examination integrity. Reasonable accommodations can alter format, timing, or access while retaining essential competencies; identical conditions are not always equitable. A low mark alone does not establish discrimination or a marking error. If concerned, keep the syllabus, published criteria, submitted work, accommodations request, result, and relevant correspondence. Ask for an explanation and use the specified review or appeal process within its deadline. Re-marking, clerical checks, and complaints about procedure can be distinct routes with different grounds. Seek reasons rather than assume a treaty guarantees a higher grade or unlimited access to confidential assessment materials.
groups.mid: A fair exam should test relevant learning, not needless barriers. Rules should be clear and used consistently. Suitable disability accommodations matter too. ICESCR Article 13 protects education. It does not set every grading, feedback, or appeal rule worldwide. Local law, school rules, and equality rights give the details. Ask about format, the marks for each part, criteria, allowed resources, deadlines, misconduct rules, and reasons for the result. Access to marked work or examiners' notes can have legal limits. Other people's rights and exam integrity matter. Reasonable adjustments may change timing, format, or access while keeping essential skills. Identical conditions are not always fair. A low mark alone does not prove bias or error. Keep the syllabus, criteria, your work, adjustment request, result, and messages. Ask for reasons and meet review or appeal dates. A clerical check, re-mark, and procedural complaint may be different routes with different grounds. A treaty does not guarantee a higher grade or every confidential assessment paper.
groups.low: A fair exam tests what you learned. It should not add needless barriers. Rules must be clear and used fairly. Suitable help for disability matters too. ICESCR Article 13 protects education. It does not set every mark, feedback, or appeal rule worldwide. Local law, school rules, and equality rights give details. Ask how the test works. How much does each part count? What skills are marked? What resources may you use? Check dates and rules on cheating. Ask why you got the mark. Access to marked work or staff notes may have legal limits. Other people's rights and exam integrity matter. Extra time or another format may help show the same essential skills. The same conditions are not always fair. A low mark alone does not prove bias or error. Keep the course plan, criteria, work, help request, marks, and messages. Ask for reasons. Use review or appeal steps on time. A sums check, re-mark, and complaint about the process may use different grounds. A treaty does not promise a higher mark. It does not promise all private papers either.
groups.source_review: Checked education and accommodation treaty principles. Specific exam procedures framed as policy-dependent rather than invented treaty clauses.
groups.notes: Corrected claims that ICESCR directly mandates every rubric/feedback/appeal format; retained practical fairness safeguards.

groups.high: Sexual harassment can undermine equal access to education and safety. CEDAW Article 10 addresses educational equality, while Committee interpretations, including General Recommendation 36 on girls' and women's education, address related barriers and violence. Article 10 does not itself contain the original claimed paragraph requiring an identical complaint committee in every institution worldwide. In Bangladesh, the High Court's 2009 BNWLA guidelines provide a specific institutional complaint-committee framework, including at least five members, a majority of women, and at least two external members, subject to the applicable legal framework. This domestic source must not be replaced by a fabricated CEDAW provision or confused with Recommendation 34 on rural women. Effective procedures require accessible reporting, prompt impartial assessment, protection against retaliation, appropriate confidentiality, and fair treatment of all parties. Confidentiality has legal and procedural limits and cannot be promised absolutely. Preserve relevant messages and details without unsafe confrontation; seek immediate safety and medical care if necessary. Ask the institution for its policy, committee contacts, support options, and complaint or appeal deadlines. Internal procedures do not automatically replace criminal or other legal remedies. Obtain qualified advice where there are threats, institutional conflicts, or risk of evidence loss.
groups.mid: Sexual harassment can make study unsafe and unfair. CEDAW Article 10 deals with education equality. General Recommendation 36 covers girls' and women's education, including barriers and violence. Article 10 does not set one identical complaint committee worldwide. Bangladesh has a separate source. The High Court's 2009 BNWLA guidelines set a panel framework. It needs at least five members. Most must be women, and at least two must be external. The rules that apply matter. This is not the claimed CEDAW paragraph. Recommendation 34 is about rural women, not this rule. People need safe reporting and prompt, impartial checks. They need protection from retaliation, suitable privacy, and fair treatment for all sides. Privacy has legal and process limits. Do not promise total secrecy. Keep relevant messages and facts without unsafe confrontation. Get to safety and seek medical care first if needed. Ask the school for its policy, panel contacts, and support. Check complaint and appeal dates. The school process does not automatically replace criminal or other legal remedies. Get expert advice about threats and conflicts. Ask about risk of lost evidence too.
groups.low: Sexual harassment can make school unsafe and unfair. CEDAW Article 10 covers equal education. General Recommendation 36 is about girls' and women's education, with barriers and violence. Article 10 does not set one identical complaint committee worldwide. Bangladesh has a separate source. Its High Court's 2009 BNWLA guidelines set a panel framework. It needs at least five members. Most must be women. At least two must be external. Check the local rules. This is not the claimed CEDAW paragraph. Recommendation 34 is about rural women, not this rule. People need safe reporting. Checks must be prompt and impartial. Guard against retaliation. Give suitable privacy and fair treatment to all sides. Privacy has legal and process limits. Do not promise total secrecy. Keep relevant messages and facts. Do not confront someone if unsafe. Get to safety and seek medical care first if needed. Ask the school for its policy, panel contacts, and support. Check complaint and appeal dates. The school process need not replace criminal or other legal routes. Get expert advice on threats, conflicts, or risk of lost evidence.
groups.source_review: Checked CEDAW Article10 and Bangladesh High Court primary judgment committee clauses. Local 2026 amendments or superseding instruments require separate case-specific confirmation.
groups.notes: Corrected invented treaty paragraph, wrong general recommendation, and universal committee/judicial-power claims.

groups.high: Bangladesh's constitutional provision on free and compulsory education is Article 17, not Article 25. It directs the State to establish a uniform, mass-oriented universal education system and extend free and compulsory education to all children to the stage determined by law. It also addresses relating education to society's needs and removing illiteracy within a legally determined time. Article 17 belongs to the fundamental principles of State policy; Article 8(2) makes those principles guides to governance and lawmaking but not directly judicially enforceable by themselves. This distinction does not erase statutory duties or other enforceable rights. Specific ages, grades, attendance duties, fees, exemptions, and enforcement must come from the applicable education legislation and rules, not be invented from Article 17 alone. ICESCR Article 13 also recognizes compulsory primary education available free to all. Implementing these commitments requires schools, teachers, accessible environments, materials, and support for excluded children, not merely a statement that attendance is mandatory. Parents should check local enrollment and lawful charges with the relevant education authority. Preserve notices and receipts and seek assistance if cost or discrimination blocks access. Do not assume every charge is lawful or every constitutional principle carries an automatic penalty.
groups.mid: Bangladesh's Constitution has free and compulsory education in Article 17, not Article 25. The State should build one system that serves the whole public and reaches all. Free schooling that children must attend should reach all children to the stage set by law. Article 17 also covers learning suited to society's needs. It calls for ending illiteracy, the lack of reading and writing skills, in a time set by law. It is a State-policy principle. Article 8(2) says such principles guide how the country is run and laws are made. They cannot be used in court by themselves. Other legal duties and rights may still apply. Exact ages, grades, attendance, fees, who may be excused, and penalties need the actual school laws and rules. Do not infer them all from Article 17. ICESCR Article 13 also calls for primary schooling free and compulsory for all. This needs schools, teachers, places all can use, materials, and help for excluded children. Saying attendance is compulsory is not enough. Ask the education office about joining school and lawful charges. Keep notices and receipts. Seek help if cost or discrimination blocks access. Not every charge is lawful. A policy principle does not carry a fixed penalty.
groups.low: Bangladesh's Constitution has a free-school rule in Article 17, not Article 25. The State should build one system that serves the whole public and reaches all. Free schooling that children must attend should reach all children to the stage set by law. Article 17 also calls for learning suited to society's needs. It calls for ending illiteracy, the lack of reading and writing skills, in a time set by law. This is a State-policy principle. Article 8(2) says these principles guide how the State is run and laws are made. They cannot be used in court by themselves. Other legal duties and rights may still apply. Exact ages, grades, attendance, fees, who may be excused, and penalties need school laws and rules. Article 17 alone does not give them all. ICESCR Article 13 calls for primary schooling free and compulsory for all. Children need schools, teachers, places all can use, materials, and help if excluded. Just saying school is compulsory is not enough. Ask the education office about joining school and lawful charges. Keep notices and receipts. Get help if cost or unfair treatment blocks access. A charge is not always lawful. A policy principle has no fixed penalty.
groups.source_review: Checked Bangladesh Articles17 and8(2) plus ICESCR13; no invented compulsory-school ages or parent penalties.
groups.notes: Corrected Article25 citation and direct-enforceability claim; separated constitutional policy from implementing statute.
